Take-home Exercise 3

Author

Tan Zong Yin Shawn

Published

November 13, 2025

Modified

November 16, 2025

Overview

Housing is an essential component of household wealth worldwide. Purchasing a home has always represented a major investment for most individuals. The price of housing is influenced by a wide range of factors. Some are macro-level, such as the overall state of the economy or the inflation rate, while others are property-specific. These can be further categorized into structural and locational factors.

Structural factors refer to the characteristics of the property itself, such as size, fittings, and tenure. Locational factors, on the other hand, relate to the neighbourhood context of the property, including proximity to childcare centres, public transport, and shopping facilities.

Traditionally, housing resale price models have been estimated using the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) method. However, this approach does not account for spatial autocorrelation and spatial heterogeneity, which are commonly present in geographic datasets such as housing transactions. When spatial autocorrelation exists, OLS estimation of housing resale price models may produce biased, inconsistent, or inefficient results (Anselin, 1998). To address these limitations, Geographically Weighted Models (GWMs) have been introduced to more accurately calibrate both explanatory and predictive models for housing resale prices.

Datasets

  • MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL: URA Master Plan 2014 subzone boundary GIS data. This data set is downloaded from Singapore’s open data portal.

  • ELDERCARE: GIS data showing location of eldercare service. This data set is downloaded from data.gov.sg.

  • RapidTransitSystemStation: SHP file with the locations of all MRT stations. This data set is downloaded from datamall.lta.gov.sg

  • Parks: geojson file with locations of all parks in singapore. This data set is downloaded from data.gov.sg.

  • HawkerCentresGEOJSON: geojson file with locations of all hawker centres in singapore. This data set is downloaded from data.gov.sg.

  • Generalinformationofschools: csv file with information of all schools in singapore. This data set is downloaded from data.gov.sg.

  • BusStop: SHP file with the locations of all bus stops. This data set is downloaded from datamall.lta.gov.sg

  • Supermarkets (GEOJSON): geojson file with locations of all supermarkets in singapore. This data set is downloaded from data.gov.sg.

  • singapore_malls_pois: csv file with information of all shopping malls in singapore. This data set is downloaded from data.gov.sg.

  • Kindergartens: geojson file with locations of all supermarkets in singapore. This data set is downloaded from data.gov.sg.

  • ListingofCentres: csv file with information of all childcare centres in singapore. This data set is downloaded from data.gov.sg.

Installing and Loading the R packages

The following code chunk will be used to load the R packages which we will require for our analysis.

pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse, readr, sp, httr, jsonlite, dplyr, purrr, ggplot2, ggcorrplot, spdep, GWmodel, olsrr, SpatialML, tmap, rsample, Metrics, units, matrixStats, corrplot, ggpubr, ggstatsplot)

Preparation of the data

Map Data

The code chunk below removes subzones that fall outside the main island of Singapore, such as the Western Islands, North-Eastern Islands and the Southern Group. These areas do not contain HDB resale transactions and are therefore excluded to streamline the analysis.

mpsz_main <- mpsz %>%
  filter(
    PLN_AREA_N != "WESTERN ISLANDS",
    PLN_AREA_N != "NORTH-EASTERN ISLANDS",
    SUBZONE_N != "SOUTHERN GROUP"
  )

We check to confirm that our object only contains the main island using the following code chunk.

tm_shape(mpsz_main) + 
  tm_polygons()

Resale price data

We will be using 4 room flats in our analysis. Below is the code chunk to filter leaving only the 4 room flats and the period from 1 January 2025 to 30 September 2025.

resale_2025_4rm <- resale %>%
  filter(month >= "2025-01" & month <= "2025-09",
         flat_type == "4 ROOM")
geocode <- function(block, streetname) {
  base_url <- "https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search"
  address <- paste(block, streetname, sep = " ")
  query <- list(
    "searchVal" = address,
    "returnGeom" = "Y",
    "getAddrDetails" = "N",
    "pageNum" = "1"
  )

  res <- GET(base_url, query = query)
  restext <- content(res, as = "text")

  output <- fromJSON(restext) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    select(results.LATITUDE, results.LONGITUDE)

  return(output)
}
resale_2025_4rm$LATITUDE  <- 0
resale_2025_4rm$LONGITUDE <- 0

for (i in 1:nrow(resale_2025_4rm)) {
  temp_output <- geocode(resale_2025_4rm[i, "block"],
                         resale_2025_4rm[i, "street_name"])
  
  resale_2025_4rm$LATITUDE[i]  <- temp_output$results.LATITUDE[1]
  resale_2025_4rm$LONGITUDE[i] <- temp_output$results.LONGITUDE[1]
}

write_rds(resale_2025_4rm, "data/rds/resale_4rm_geo.rds")
resale_4rm_sf <- read_rds("data/rds/resale_4rm_geo.rds") %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(svy21)

Primary school data

The code chunk below filters the schools dataset to include only primary schools which we will use in our analysis.

schools_primary <- schools %>%
  filter(mainlevel_code == "PRIMARY")
schools_primary$LATITUDE  <- 0
schools_primary$LONGITUDE <- 0

for (i in 1:nrow(schools_primary)) {
  temp_output <- geocode(schools_primary[i, "postal_code"], "")
  
  schools_primary$LATITUDE[i]  <- temp_output$results.LATITUDE[1]
  schools_primary$LONGITUDE[i] <- temp_output$results.LONGITUDE[1]
}

write_rds(schools_primary, "data/rds/schools_primary_geo.rds")
schools_primary_sf <- read_rds("data/rds/schools_primary_geo.rds") %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(svy21)

Childcare centre data

The code chunk below filters the childcare centre dataset to include only centres that were last updated between January and September 2025.

childcare_2025 <- childcare %>%
  mutate(last_updated = as.Date(last_updated, format = "%d/%m/%Y")) %>%
  filter(
    last_updated >= as.Date("2025-01-01"),
    last_updated <= as.Date("2025-09-30")
  )

childcare_2025$LATITUDE  <- 0
childcare_2025$LONGITUDE <- 0

for (i in 1:nrow(childcare_2025)) {
  temp_output <- geocode(childcare_2025[i, "postal_code"], "")
  
  childcare_2025$LATITUDE[i]  <- temp_output$results.LATITUDE[1]
  childcare_2025$LONGITUDE[i] <- temp_output$results.LONGITUDE[1]
}

write_rds(childcare_2025, "data/rds/childcare_geo.rds")
childcare_sf <- read_rds("data/rds/childcare_geo.rds") %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(svy21)

MRT data

The Rapid Transit System dataset includes various railway-related geometries such as LRT features, depots and viaducts polygons. To extract only the actual MRT stations, we apply two filters:

  1. TYP_CD_DES must be “MRT”

  2. STN_NAM_DE must contain the word “STATION”

mrt <- mrt %>%
  filter(
    TYP_CD_DES == "MRT",
    grepl("STATION", STN_NAM_DE, ignore.case = TRUE)
  )

Checking for z dimensions

Spatial objects may occasionally contain a Z-dimension (elevation values). Since our current require
2-dimensional geometries, it is important to ensure that all sf layers are stored as XY coordinates.

To streamline this process, we create two helper functions:

  1. check_z() - inspects whether an sf object contains a Z-dimension.
  2. drop_z_if_exists() - removes the Z-dimension only if it is present.

These functions help us efficiently verify and clean all spatial layers.

check_z <- function(sf_object) {
  coords <- st_coordinates(sf_object)
  
  if ("Z" %in% colnames(coords)) {
    message("Z-dimension detected in: ", deparse(substitute(sf_object)))
  } else {
    message("No Z-dimension in: ", deparse(substitute(sf_object)))
  }
  
  return(head(coords))
}

drop_z_if_exists <- function(sf_object) {
  coords <- st_coordinates(sf_object)
  
  if ("Z" %in% colnames(coords)) {
    message("Removing Z-dimension from: ", deparse(substitute(sf_object)))
    return(st_zm(sf_object))
  } else {
    message("Already in 2D: ", deparse(substitute(sf_object)))
    return(sf_object)
  }
}

All spatial datasets were examined for the presence of Z-coordinates. The results show that most layers are already stored in 2-dimensional XY format. For those with Z-values, the st_zm() function was applied to remove the extra dimension. This ensures that subsequent spatial operations are performed correctly without dimensional conflicts.

Important

The MRT station output includes extra columns named L1, L2, L3. These columns do not represent spatial coordinates. Instead, they are index identifiers that tell us which part of the geometry the coordinate belongs to.

L1 refers to the main ring or holes, L2 to the ring id in the MULTIPOLYGON, and L3 to the simple feature. Multipolygon

Handling multipolygons

To ensure a clean and consistent point layer for our analysis, we convert polygons into representative point features using st_point_on_surface().

mrt <- st_point_on_surface(mrt)

Checking for overlapping data

Due to the nature of high-rise HDB housing, multiple transactions may originate from the same block and therefore share identical coordinates. When these overlapping points remain unresolved, certain spatial operations may encounter instability or numerical issues.

To ensure smooth modelling, we first detect overlapping points and subsequently apply a small jitter to separate them by up to 1 metre. This adjustment is spatially negligible but prevents computational conflicts in later stages.

overlapping_points <- resale_4rm_sf %>%
  mutate(overlap = lengths(st_equals(., .)) > 1)
set.seed(1234)
resale_4rm_sf <- resale_4rm_sf %>%
  st_jitter(amount = 1)

Data wrangling

Storey range conversion

Two key housing attributes, storey_range and remaining_lease, are supplied in textual formats that are not suitable for statistical modelling. To make these variables usable in our regression and geographically weighted regression models, they are transformed into continuous numeric measures.

The storey_range field is expressed as a range (for example, “01 TO 03”). For analysis, the range is split into its lower and upper bounds, and the midpoint of the range is computed to represent the typical floor level of the flat. This produces a single numeric variable (storey_mid) that is easy to interpret and can be used directly in regression models.

resale_4rm_sf <- resale_4rm_sf %>%
  mutate(
    storey_low  = as.numeric(str_extract(storey_range, "^\\d+")),
    storey_high = as.numeric(str_extract(storey_range, "(?<= TO )\\d+")),
    storey_mid  = (storey_low + storey_high) / 2
    )

Remaining lease conversion

The remaining_lease field is provided in a descriptive form such as “93 years 10 months”. The numeric components are extracted, and the years and months are combined into a single continuous measure expressed in years (remaining_lease_yrs). This allows the remaining lease to be incorporated as a quantitative predictor without losing information.

resale_4rm_sf <- resale_4rm_sf %>%
  mutate(
    lease_nums = str_extract_all(remaining_lease, "\\d+"),
    lease_years = vapply(lease_nums, function(x) as.numeric(x[1]), numeric(1)),
    lease_months = vapply(lease_nums, function(x) {
      if (length(x) >= 2) as.numeric(x[2]) else 0
    }, numeric(1)),
    remaining_lease_yrs = lease_years + lease_months / 12
  ) %>%
  select(-lease_nums, -lease_years, -lease_months)

Transaction date conversion

The transaction month in the resale dataset is supplied in the format “YYYY-MM”, which is a character field rather than a true date object. To make the variable usable for trend analysis and later modelling, the string is converted into a proper date by appending the first day of the month and running it through as.Date(). From this, the transaction year and month are extracted as numeric fields. These derived variables allow us to capture possible temporal effects in the resale prices and ensure that the modelling dataset contains consistently formatted date information.

resale_4rm_sf <- resale_4rm_sf %>%
  mutate(
    sale_date = as.Date(paste0(month, "-01")),
    sale_year = as.numeric(format(sale_date, "%Y")),
    sale_month = as.numeric(format(sale_date, "%m"))
  )

Age of unit computation

After converting the transaction month into a proper date format, the next structural variable prepared is the age of the unit. Although the HDB resale dataset does not directly provide the age of each flat, it includes information on remaining lease. Since most HDB flats are sold under a 99-year lease, the age of the unit can be derived as Age of Unit = 99 – Remaining Lease.

resale_4rm_sf <- resale_4rm_sf %>%
  mutate(
    age_of_unit = 99 - remaining_lease_yrs
  )

Computing proximity measures

To study how accessibility influences resale flat prices, distance-based variables are created to capture the proximity of each flat to nearby amenities. The distance between every 4-room resale flat and each category of amenity is computed using st_distance(). For each amenity type, the minimum distance is taken to represent the nearest available facility. This yields a set of continuous explanatory variables such as distance to the nearest MRT station, childcare centre and kindergarten.

The below code chunk is a reusable function that will be used to calculate the proximity distance.

nearest_dist <- function(from_pts, to_pts) {
  st_distance(from_pts, to_pts) %>%
    apply(1, min) %>% 
    as.numeric()
}
resale_4rm_sf <- resale_4rm_sf %>%
  mutate(
    dist_mrt = nearest_dist(., mrt),
    dist_school_pri = nearest_dist(., schools_primary_sf),
    dist_childcare = nearest_dist(., childcare_sf),
    dist_kinder = nearest_dist(., kindergartens),
    dist_mall = nearest_dist(., malls),
    dist_busstop = nearest_dist(., busstop),
    dist_eldercare = nearest_dist(., eldercare),
    dist_hawker = nearest_dist(., hawkers),
    dist_park = nearest_dist(., parks),
    dist_supermarket = nearest_dist(., supermarkets)
  )

Computing neighbourhood counts within distance

Beyond measuring the nearest distance, accessibility is also captured through the number of amenities available within a reasonable walking radius. Such variables represent local opportunity density and are commonly used in hedonic pricing and spatial accessibility studies.

The below code chunk is a reusable function that will be used to calculate the number of amenities within a set distance.

count_within <- function(from_pts, to_pts, radius) {
  hits_list <- st_is_within_distance(from_pts, to_pts, dist = radius)
  sapply(hits_list, length)
}

Each 4-room resale flat is buffered by a specified radius (350m/1km), and the number of surrounding amenities falling inside the buffer is counted. This produces variables such as the number of kindergartens within 350m, number of childcare centres within 350m, number of bus stops within 350m and number of primary schools within 1km. These neighbourhood measures are attached to the resale dataset as part of the data wrangling process to be used later.

resale_4rm_sf <- resale_4rm_sf %>%
  mutate(
    n_kinder_350m     = count_within(., kindergartens, radius = 350),
    n_childcare_350m  = count_within(., childcare_sf, radius = 350),
    n_busstop_350m    = count_within(., busstop, radius = 350),
    n_schoolpri_1km   = count_within(., schools_primary_sf, radius = 1000)
  )

Exploratory Analysis

Before building the Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) model, an exploratory analysis was conducted to understand the structure, distribution, and spatial patterns of the variables used in the study.

This step ensures that:

  • the predictors are meaningful and non-redundant

  • the relationships between variables are reasonable

  • the data contains spatial variation that justifies using GWR instead of a global model

  • potential issues such as multicollinearity, outliers, or skewness are identified early

The exploratory analysis focuses on the prepared 4-room resale HDB dataset (resale_4rm_sf) and its associated amenity proximity variables.

Distribution of Key Variables

Structural Factors

Structural factors describe the physical characteristics and intrinsic attributes of the HDB unit. These variables directly influence resale value because they affect the usable space, housing quality, lifespan and overall desirability of the flat.

p_area <- ggplot(resale_4rm_sf, aes(x = floor_area_sqm)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Floor Area (sqm)", x = "Floor area (sqm)", y = "Count")

p_storey <- ggplot(resale_4rm_sf, aes(x = storey_range)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "darkorange", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Floor Level (Storey Range)", x = "Storey range", y = "Count") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

p_lease <- ggplot(resale_4rm_sf, aes(x = remaining_lease_yrs)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "salmon", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Remaining Lease (Years)", x = "Remaining lease (years)", y = "Count")

p_age <- ggplot(resale_4rm_sf, aes(x = age_of_unit)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "seagreen", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Age of Unit (Years)", x = "Age of unit (years)", y = "Count")

ggarrange(p_area, p_storey, p_lease, p_age, ncol = 2, nrow = 2)

The distribution of floor area for 4-room flats is tightly centred around the 90–100 sqm range, with a strong peak at approximately 95 sqm. This reflects standardised HDB flat designs, where most 4-room layouts fall within a narrow band. A small number of larger units (110–120 sqm) and smaller units (<90 sqm) exist but occur infrequently.

Storey levels show a right-skewed distribution, with most flats located between the 1st and 15th storey. Mid-level floors (7th to 13th storey) dominate the dataset, consistent with Singapore’s typical HDB block height profile. Higher floors (above 25th storey) form only a small proportion of the sample.

Remaining lease exhibits a multi-modal distribution, reflecting clusters of older and newer estates. Many units have between 55–65 years of lease remaining, corresponding to older precincts built in the 1980s–1990s. A second concentration occurs around 80–90 years, representing newer flats launched after the mid-2000s.

Age distribution ranges from newly built flats (<10 years old) to mature blocks exceeding 40 years. This variation indicates that age is a strong structural factor, capturing depreciation, estate maturity and buyer expectations of older neighbourhoods.

Location factors

Distance Based

Distance-based variables capture how close each flat is to key amenities and activity centres. In this study, proximity is measured from every resale flat to the nearest MRT station, park, hawker centre/food court, shopping mall, supermarket and eldercare facility. Since all distances are computed using the SVY21 projected coordinate system, so the results are expressed in metres and are directly interpretable as walking or travel distance.

p_elder <- ggplot(resale_4rm_sf, aes(x = dist_eldercare)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "darkorange", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distance to Eldercare", x = "Distance (m)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_hawker <- ggplot(resale_4rm_sf, aes(x = dist_hawker)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "firebrick", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distance to Hawker Centre", x = "Distance (m)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_mrt <- ggplot(resale_4rm_sf, aes(x = dist_mrt)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "purple", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distance to MRT", x = "Distance (m)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_park <- ggplot(resale_4rm_sf, aes(x = dist_park)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "forestgreen", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distance to Park", x = "Distance (m)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_mall <- ggplot(resale_4rm_sf, aes(x = dist_mall)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "goldenrod", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distance to Shopping Mall", x = "Distance (m)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_super <- ggplot(resale_4rm_sf, aes(x = dist_supermarket)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "turquoise4", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distance to Supermarket", x = "Distance (m)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

ggarrange(p_elder, p_hawker, p_mrt, p_park,  p_mall, p_super,
  ncol = 2, nrow = 3
)

Eldercare distribution shows a clear right-skew, with a large concentration of units within 400-800m of an eldercare centre. This suggests that eldercare services are spatially well distributed across Singapore’s residential areas. Only a small proportion of units lie more than 2 km away.

Distances to hawker centres cluster tightly around 300-800m, with long tails beyond 1.5 km. This indicates that most households can access food options within a short walk, while only a minority are located relatively far from these amenities.

MRT proximity shows a strong mode around 400-700m, gradually tapering toward 2km. Relatively few flats have extremely close MRT access (<200m), while some peripheral or older estates remain further away.

Distance to parks exhibits wider spread, mostly within 400-1200m, reflecting the mix of small neighbourhood parks and larger regional parks.

Most units are within 400-900m of a mall, with a decreasing tail extending toward 2 km and beyond.

Supermarkets show the shortest distances overall, with a heavy concentration around 200-500m. Only a small number of units fall beyond 1km from a supermarket.

Across all amenities, the distributions confirm Singapore’s compact urban layout, where key facilities are commonly reachable within 5-10min of walking.

Count Based

The distributions of these count variables reveal how richly served different neighbourhoods are. Flats in mature or highly developed estates tend to have more childcare centres, kindergartens and bus stops within 350 m, and more primary schools within 1 km, whereas units in newer or less dense areas often have fewer nearby facilities.

p_kinder <- ggplot(resale_4rm_sf, aes(n_kinder_350m)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#FFA500", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Kindergartens Within 350m", x = "Count", y = "Frequency")

p_childcare <- ggplot(resale_4rm_sf, aes(n_childcare_350m)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#FF6F61", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Childcare Centres Within 350m", x = "Count", y = "Frequency")

p_busstops <- ggplot(resale_4rm_sf, aes(n_busstop_350m)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#1E90FF", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Bus Stops Within 350m", x = "Count", y = "Frequency")

p_schoolpri <- ggplot(resale_4rm_sf, aes(n_schoolpri_1km)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#32CD32", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Primary Schools Within 1km", x = "Count", y = "Frequency")

ggarrange(p_kinder, p_childcare, p_busstops, p_schoolpri,ncol = 2, nrow = 2)

Kindergartens within 350m is strongly right-skewed, with most flats having 0 to 3 kindergartens nearby. Only a small portion of units have very high counts (5 or more), reflecting concentrated early-childhood education clusters in certain estates.

Childcare centres show a similar pattern, with most flats having 1 to 4 centres within short walking distance. A long right tail indicates highly service-rich neighbourhoods.

Bus stop counts are the highest among all categories, commonly ranging from 2 to 6 bus stops within 350m. This is expected due to the dense bus network. The spread also reflects flats located near bus interchanges or multiple bus corridors.

Most flats fall within 0 to 3 primary schools within 1km, with some areas near schooling clusters reaching higher values.

Correlation Matrix

The correlation matrix provides an initial view of how the structural and locational variables relate to each other and to the resale prices. This step is part of exploratory data analysis and helps identify broad relationships before moving to more detailed modelling.

vars_struct_loc <- c(
  "resale_price",
  "floor_area_sqm",
  "age_of_unit",
  "remaining_lease_yrs",
  "n_schoolpri_1km",
  "n_kinder_350m",
  "n_childcare_350m",
  "n_busstop_350m",
  "dist_mrt",
  "dist_mall",
  "dist_supermarket",
  "dist_hawker",
  "dist_park",
  "dist_eldercare"
)

cor_mat <- resale_4rm_sf %>% 
  st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  select(all_of(vars_struct_loc)) %>% 
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
ggcorrplot(
  cor_mat,
  type       = "lower",
  lab        = FALSE, 
  outline.col = "white",
  hc.order   = FALSE
) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    limits = c(-1, 1),
    breaks = seq(-1, 1, 0.5),
    name   = "Pearson r"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Matrix of Structural and Locational Variables",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title  = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid  = element_blank()
  )

The correlation matrix shows that most structural and locational variables exhibit only weak relationships with one another, indicating that these factors tend to vary independently across 4-room HDB resale flats. As expected, the strongest relationship is between age of unit and remaining lease years, which display a strong negative correlation because older flats naturally have fewer years left on their lease. Apart from this, structural characteristics such as resale price and floor area show minimal association with locational attributes, suggesting that price and size differences are not strongly driven by proximity to amenities within this flat type.

Among the locational variables, amenity counts show mild positive correlations with one another. This reflects the clustering of child-centric facilities in denser residential areas. In contrast, the distance-based variables show very weak correlations with both structural features and amenity counts, indicating that accessibility to larger amenities like MRT stations, malls, supermarkets, hawker centres, parks or eldercare facilities is relatively uncorrelated with flat-level characteristics.

Overall, the weak correlations suggest that no single factor dominates on its own and prices are better understood using a multivariate model rather than simple pairwise relationships.

Hedonic Pricing Model

A global hedonic pricing model was constructed to examine the relationship between resale flat prices and a set of structural and locational attributes. Structural predictors include floor area and remaining lease years, while locational attributes capture the availability and accessibility of key amenities. The global model provides the baseline effects of each variable across the study area and serves as the starting point for spatial diagnostics and subsequent GWR analysis.

Linear Regression

The following code chunk will be used to create our model.

vars_final <- c(
  "resale_price",
  "floor_area_sqm",
  "remaining_lease_yrs",
  "n_schoolpri_1km",
  "n_kinder_350m",
  "n_childcare_350m",
  "n_busstop_350m",
  "dist_mrt",
  "dist_mall",
  "dist_supermarket",
  "dist_hawker",
  "dist_park",
  "dist_eldercare"
)

resale_4rm_model <- resale_4rm_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(all_of(vars_final))
hpm.lm <- lm(
  resale_price ~ .,
  data = resale_4rm_model
)

summary(hpm.lm)

The model explains approximately 60% of the variation in 4-room resale flat prices, indicating that the structural and locational variables included in the model capture a substantial portion of price determinants. Among the structural attributes, floor area and remaining lease years exhibit strong and positive influences on resale price, reflecting buyers’ preference for larger units and longer lease durations.

Locational factors also play an important role. Proximity to key amenities is consistently associated with higher resale prices, as indicated by the negative coefficients for all distance variables. Prices decrease as distance to these amenities increases. The amenity count variables reveal a more nuanced pattern. A higher number of kindergartens within walking distance is associated with higher prices, suggesting added value from child-friendly environments.

However, greater densities of childcare centres, bus stops, or primary schools tend to correlate with lower resale prices, which may reflect neighbourhood characteristics such as older built-up areas, higher traffic intensity, or greater congestion.

Overall, the global model provides a clear understanding of the average relationships between housing attributes and resale prices across the study area. However, because these effects may vary spatially, the global model serves as a baseline for subsequent spatial diagnostics and geographically weighted regression to examine local variations in these relationships.

Moran’s I

We extract the residuals from the global hedonic pricing model hpm.lm. These residuals represent the portion of resale price variation not explained by the structural and locational predictors. In spatial analysis, examining residuals is essential because spatial clustering in the unexplained component may indicate that the our model has missed important spatial processes.

hpm.resid <- residuals(hpm.lm)

A spatial weights matrix is constructed to define the neighbourhood structure among resale flats. A 6-nearest-neighbour scheme is used, ensuring that each observation has a consistent number of spatial neighbours.

coords <- st_coordinates(resale_4rm_sf)

knn6 <- knearneigh(coords, k = 6)
nb6 <- knn2nb(knn6)

lw6 <- nb2listw(nb6, style = "W")

The Moran’s I test is performed on the OLS residuals using the spatial weights matrix created earlier. This test assesses whether the residuals are spatially clustered or randomly distributed. A significant Moran’s I statistic would indicate positive spatial autocorrelation, suggesting that the global OLS model does not adequately capture spatial dependence or spatially varying relationships. This diagnostic provides the justification for advancing to local modelling techniques such as Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR).

hpm.moran <- moran.test(hpm.resid, lw6)
hpm.moran

    Moran I test under randomisation

data:  hpm.resid  
weights: lw6    

Moran I statistic standard deviate = 144.57, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
     8.409268e-01     -1.152339e-04      3.384352e-05

The Moran’s I test reveals strong and highly significant spatial autocorrelation in the residuals of the global hedonic price model. The Moran’s I statistic is 0.839, which is extremely high for residuals, and the associated p-value is < 2.2e-16, indicating that the observed clustering is far greater than would be expected under spatial randomness. This result shows that our model does not fully account for spatial patterns in resale prices and that important spatial processes remain in the unexplained component of the model.

The presence of strong positive spatial autocorrelation means that nearby flats tend to have similar residual values. This violates the OLS assumption of independent errors and signals that the relationships between price and the explanatory variables are spatially non-stationary.

Geographically Weighted Regression

Bandwidth Selection

The optimal bandwidth for the GWR model is identified using the AICc-based adaptive bandwidth selection procedure provided by bw.gwr(). An adaptive bisquare kernel is employed to ensure that each local regression calibrates using a consistent number of neighbouring observations, which is suitable given the uneven spatial distribution of resale flats across Singapore. The bandwidth parameter determines the spatial extent over which local relationships are estimated, and selecting it through AICc minimises model complexity while maximising explanatory power. This step establishes the spatial scale at which the relationships between resale price and its predictors vary across the study area.

gwr.bw <- bw.gwr(
  formula  = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
                             remaining_lease_yrs +
                             n_schoolpri_1km +
                             n_kinder_350m +
                             n_childcare_350m +
                             n_busstop_350m +
                             dist_mrt +
                             dist_mall +
                             dist_supermarket +
                             dist_hawker +
                             dist_park +
                             dist_eldercare,
  data     = resale_4rm_sf,
  approach = "AICc",
  kernel   = "bisquare",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat  = FALSE
)

gwr.bw
write_rds(gwr.bw, "data/rds/gwr_bw.rds")
gwr.bw <- readRDS("data/rds/gwr_bw.rds")

Constructing the adaptive bandwidth gwr model

Based on the optimal adaptive bandwidth identified, the GWR model will then be calibrated using this bandwidth. The same set of structural and locational predictors from the linear regression model was included so that the results remain directly comparable.

hpm.gwr <- gwr.basic(
  formula  = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
                             remaining_lease_yrs +
                             n_schoolpri_1km +
                             n_kinder_350m +
                             n_childcare_350m +
                             n_busstop_350m +
                             dist_mrt +
                             dist_mall +
                             dist_supermarket +
                             dist_hawker +
                             dist_park +
                             dist_eldercare,
  data     = resale_4rm_sf,
  bw       = gwr.bw,
  kernel   = "bisquare",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat  = FALSE
)

The GWR model provides a much better fit than the linear regression model, showing that the factors influencing resale prices vary across different parts of Singapore. The adjusted R² increases from about 0.61 in the linear regression model to 0.94 in the GWR model, and the AICc drops sharply from 224,643 to 209,041 which indicates a significantly improved model. The large reduction in residual errors also shows that GWR captures local pricing patterns far more accurately.

The wide range of GWR coefficient values suggests that the impact of each variable changes depending on the location. For example, floor area and remaining lease have much stronger positive effects in some neighbourhoods, while the influence of nearby amenities varies according to local demand and estate characteristics.

Overall, the GWR results confirm that the housing market is not uniform across Singapore. Different neighbourhoods value attributes differently, and allowing the model to vary locally provides a much clearer picture of how prices are shaped across space.

Note

The linear regression model was used as the baseline regression. Moran’s I was then applied to the residuals to check for spatial autocorrelation. The significant Moran’s I result indicated that the base linear regression model does not fully capture spatial patterns, providing justification for applying our GWR.

In other neighbourhoods, the effect is negative. This confirms that eldercare amenities influence prices differently across demographic profiles and neighbourhood designs.

  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey70", lwd = 0.5) +
tm_shape(resale_4rm_sf) +
  tm_dots(
    fill = "n_schoolpri_1km",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      n = 5,
      values = "YlOrRd"
    ),
    size = 0.1
  ) +
tm_title("Local Effect of Primary Schools (1km)")

The effect of primary school count varies widely across the island. Some regions show a positive coefficient, where having more schools nearby increases resale value. However, large clusters display negative effects, suggesting that school density can also introduce congestion or competition, lowering perceived amenity value. This spatially mixed pattern illustrates that school accessibility is not universally beneficial and depends on neighbourhood context.

tm_shape(mpsz_main) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey70", lwd = 0.5) +
tm_shape(resale_4rm_sf) +
  tm_dots(
    fill = "n_kinder_350m",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      n = 5,
      values = "YlOrRd"
    ),
    size = 0.1
  ) +
tm_title("Local Effect of Kindergartens (350m)")

Kindergarten availability shows highly localised effects. Certain central and northeastern estates exhibit strong positive coefficients, indicating that proximity to preschool options boosts housing demand. Conversely, some areas show negative or weak effects, likely the same reason as primary schools

tm_shape(mpsz_main) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey70", lwd = 0.5) +
tm_shape(resale_4rm_sf) +
  tm_dots(
    fill = "n_childcare_350m",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      n = 5,
      values = "YlOrRd"
    ),
    size = 0.1
  ) +
tm_title("Local Effect of Childcare Centres (350m)")

Childcare centres display mixed but generally modest impacts on resale prices. Positive effects appear in estates with a high concentration of young families, suggesting increased convenience value. In other areas, negative effects may indicate saturation or perceived crowding.

tm_shape(mpsz_main) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey70", lwd = 0.5) +
tm_shape(resale_4rm_sf) +
  tm_dots(
    fill = "n_busstop_350m",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      n = 5,
      values = "YlOrRd"
    ),
    size = 0.05
  ) +
tm_title("Local Effect of Bus Stops (350m)")

The local effect of bus stop density is mostly negative, though the strength varies. Areas with strong negative coefficients may be experiencing noise, traffic, or bus activity that slightly reduces housing desirability. In contrast, weaker or near-zero effects occur in regions where public transport is expected and normalized.

The GWR results show that the factors affecting 4-room HDB resale prices vary across different parts of Singapore rather than behaving the same everywhere. Structural factors such as floor area and remaining lease have the strongest impact in the central region, where buyers place higher value on larger units and longer leases. Their influence becomes more moderate in the western and northern areas.

Accessibility factors like distance to MRT stations are most important in the eastern and northeastern regions, where rail access plays a larger role in daily travel. Locational amenities such as malls, supermarkets, hawker centres, parks and eldercare facilities also show stronger effects in the eastern, northeastern and western parts of the island, where such amenities are less concentrated. In contrast, the central region sees weaker effects because amenities are already abundant.

Family-related amenities, including schools and childcare centres, matter more in the eastern and northeastern regions, which tend to have younger households. Overall, the results highlight that different regions respond differently to the same housing attributes, and resale prices are shaped by localised preferences rather than a single island-wide pattern.

GWR Residual Map

The residual map provides a spatial view of where the GWR model still under or over predicts resale prices. The code chunk below will be used to plot our residual map.

tm_shape(mpsz_main) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "grey95",
    col  = "grey70",
    lwd  = 0.5
  ) +
tm_shape(resale_4rm_sf) +
  tm_dots(
    fill = "residual",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style  = "quantile",
      n      = 5,
      values = "-RdBu"
    ),
    size = 0.08
  ) +
tm_title("Residuals of GWR Model")

Most areas show small residual values, reflecting that the GWR model explains a large proportion of price variation after accounting for spatially varying relationships. A few clusters of higher positive or negative residuals remain, indicating locations where additional unmeasured factors may influence prices. Overall, the residual pattern is much weaker and more dispersed compared to the OLS residuals, confirming that GWR successfully reduces spatial bias and improves the model fit.

Conclusion

This study examined the spatial drivers of 4-room HDB resale prices using Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR). The results show that housing attributes do not influence prices uniformly across Singapore; instead, their effects vary significantly by location. Structural factors such as floor area and remaining lease have the strongest impact in the central region, where demand pressures are higher. Their influence weakens gradually towards the western and northern areas.

Accessibility and amenity-related variables, including distance to MRT stations, parks, hawker centres and supermarkets, show stronger effects in the eastern, northeastern and western parts of the island, where such amenities are less concentrated. This suggests that buyers in amenity-scarce regions place greater value on proximity to daily conveniences and public transport. Family-oriented amenities like schools and childcare facilities matter more in the eastern and northeastern regions, reflecting younger household profiles in those areas.

Overall, the GWR model captures local variations far better than a global model, revealing clear spatial heterogeneity in housing price determinants. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for neighbourhood-specific dynamics in housing valuation, planning and policy design. Future work may incorporate temporal analysis, additional socio-economic variables, or alternative spatial models to further strengthen the understanding of price behaviour across Singapore.
